extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers and students interested in the Volkswagen emissions scandal and vehicle emissions regulation
extracted.subtask_short: wiki article on VW emissions scandal
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia encyclopedic article describing the Volkswagen 'Dieselgate' emissions-cheating scandal: background, technical details, investigations, recalls, legal actions, and consequences. Intended to summarize facts, timelines, regulatory standards and reactions around the event.

rubrics_metrics.name: US EPA Tier 2 / Bin 5 NOx limit
rubrics_metrics.description: The US EPA Tier 2 / Bin 5 emissions standard requires that nitrogen oxide emissions not exceed 0.07 g/mi (0.043 g/km) for engines at full useful life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full useful life is defined as either 190,000 kilometres (120,000 mi) or 240,000 kilometres (150,000 mi) depending on vehicle and certification choices. The Volkswagen/Audi cars identified as violators were certified to these standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: European Euro 5 and Euro 6 NOx limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Euro 5 (2009–2014 models) limits NOx to 0.18 g/km; Euro 6 (2015 models) limits NOx to 0.08 g/km.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These limits are less stringent than the US Tier 2/Bin 5 standard cited for some comparisons; the article uses these figures to compare on-road vs laboratory results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and prohibition of 'defeat devices' under EU/US rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'defeat device' is software or hardware that reduces effectiveness of emissions controls except under specified conditions; defeat devices are forbidden in the EU and their use is subject to penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions exist where devices are necessary to protect the engine or ensure safe operation; these exceptions create scope for interpretation. The VW engine firmware that detected testing conditions and altered emissions controls was characterized as a defeat device.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA Notice of Violation (NOV) status
rubrics_metrics.description: A Notice of Violation is a notification to the recipient that the EPA believes it has committed violations and is not a final determination of liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NOV initiated regulatory action and recalls but itself does not finalize legal liability; it triggers investigations and enforcement processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification testing protocol (FTP-75 detection criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA's FTP-75 test schedule uses specific test conditions; Volkswagen's defeat-device firmware detected signals matching the dynamometer test (steering wheel position, vehicle speed, engine duration, barometric pressure) and activated emissions controls during testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matching vehicle inputs to the test protocol allows software to detect testing conditions and behave differently in the lab versus on-road, enabling compliance during certification but excess emissions in normal operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Portable Emissions Measurement Systems (PEMS) for on-road testing
rubrics_metrics.description: PEMS make it possible to collect real-world driving emissions data for comparison with laboratory dynamometer testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICCT and WVU used PEMS to detect large deviations between laboratory and on-road NOx emissions, which was central to identifying the scandal; PEMS data were used by regulators and researchers as evidence of non-compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory recall requirements and triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: A recall is required when a defect is identified that could result in serious injury; different jurisdictions have specific recall rules. Authorities (e.g., Germany's KBA) can order full recalls and require plans from manufacturers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some countries manufacturers may offer free repairs without a formal recall if the defect is not classified as likely to cause serious injury; authorities can still require removal of illegal software and validation that emission rules are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturer obligations to ensure emissions compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturers must ensure that emission rules are fulfilled and must submit recall/fix plans to regulators (e.g., KBA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities may require removal of offending software and approval of fixes; manufacturers are expected to propose fixes that achieve legal compliance without impairing performance, though authorities perform independent testing of proposed remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable technical solutions for NOx control (SCR vs lean-NOx trap)
rubrics_metrics.description: Selective catalytic reduction (SCR) using urea (BlueTec) reduces NOx effectively but is expensive and high-maintenance; lean NOx trap (LNT) is an alternative but has drawbacks such as requiring periodic fuel-rich operation and harming fuel economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of technology involves trade-offs in cost, packaging, maintenance and fuel consumption; VW management preferred to develop an inexpensive lean NOx trap rather than license BlueTec, and technical limits of chosen solutions contributed to later decisions to manipulate software.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on use of engine management strategies that detect testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislation and guidance note that sensors and electronics can detect start of emissions tests, and functions that operate only in a predefined test mode can enable defeat devices; such detection is problematic and exceptions are tightly constrained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a substantive concern in standards: if vehicle functions are only operational in test mode, they can be tailoring emissions performance to pass laboratory tests while failing in real-world driving; regulators warned about this in research reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full useful life metric for emissions compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Emissions standards are defined for an engine's 'full useful life' (e.g., 190,000 km or 240,000 km) which determines long-term compliance expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compliance must be maintained for the defined useful life; software or hardware that causes excessive real-world emissions over the vehicle's useful life violates certification requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA / CARB certification and testing responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Vehicles must be certified to EPA or California Air Resources Board standards; regulators perform and can repeat tests and can deny certification for new models if performance in real-world tests is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators can quarantine vehicles at ports and withhold certification (as happened with 2016 models) until they are satisfied that catalysts and controls perform on the road as in tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory enforcement outcomes (fines, criminal charges, civil settlements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory and legal actions for emissions fraud can include fines, criminal pleas, indictments, large civil settlements and buybacks; VW faced billions in fines and settlements and criminal charges against executives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences vary across jurisdictions and can include corporate guilty pleas, criminal fines, executive indictments, and large-scale consumer compensation and buybacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for public disclosure and recall communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturers are expected to provide clear communications to affected customers (e.g., online VIN lookup, notification letters) and publicly disclose scope of affected vehicles and planned remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely and accurate notification to owners and regulators is required; VW set up online services for owners to check affected status and mailed rectification letters when recall plans were being implemented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical validation of proposed fixes by regulators
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed software or hardware fixes must be tested and approved by relevant authorities (e.g., KBA approved fixes for certain engines before recall rollout).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approval processes can delay recalls; independent testing may reveal effects such as reduced fuel economy or power, prompting further testing or delays (e.g., Passat fix delayed due to higher fuel consumption in tests).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of what constitutes an emissions-compliance irregularity vs illegal manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulators distinguish between irregularities (e.g., reporting errors, measurement issues) and intentional installation of devices to cheat tests; the latter constitutes illegal manipulation and can carry criminal liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations aim to determine intent and whether software was installed for a 'forbidden purpose'; Volkswagen argued some devices were 'not installed with a forbidden purpose' for some engines, but US complaints alleged automatic modes enabled non-compliant operation outside testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of independent research and transparency in uncovering non-compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent testing by bodies like ICCT and university researchers (WVU CAFEE) using real-world tests was crucial to detecting discrepancies between lab and on-road emissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open publication of on-road results and informing regulators are part of the compliance assurance ecosystem; the article highlights how independent research can trigger regulatory inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising and green-certification integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Environmental claims (e.g., 'Clean Diesel') and awards (e.g., Green Car of the Year) must reflect real-world performance; false claims can lead to rescinded awards and reputational/contractual consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media agencies and award bodies may withdraw promotion and honors when claims are shown to be misleading, and such claims may factor into consumer protection actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority powers to quarantine uncertified vehicles
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulators (EPA) can quarantine uncertified vehicles (e.g., at ports) when certification is withdrawn or questioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can strand vehicles awaiting certification and disrupt manufacturer sales and logistics until compliance is demonstrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and procedural standard that NOV is not final determination
rubrics_metrics.description: A Notice of Violation is an initial enforcement step signalling belief of violations, but is not a final determination of liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It triggers further investigation, potential recalls, negotiation, and litigation; stakeholders should treat NOVs as the start of formal enforcement rather than the final outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions in emissions law for engine protection and safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Emissions legislation allows narrow exceptions for devices necessary to protect the engine against damage or ensure safe operation; these exceptions can be invoked but are limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because exceptions are limited, their interpretation is critical; misuse of these exceptions can be judged as enabling defeat devices and lead to enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing evidence thresholds used by regulators
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulators and researchers use laboratory dynamometer tests and on-road PEMS data; large multipliers of legal limits (e.g., 5–40x) in on-road tests serve as strong evidence of non-compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated and reproducible on-road exceedances relative to certified dyno values were used to build cases prompting NOVs and recalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate governance and internal reporting expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Boards and executives are expected to be informed about major compliance issues; failures of governance (e.g., long-term concealment) attract regulatory and public scrutiny and may produce criminal investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents allegations that management knew of issues for years; strong governance, internal audits, and transparency are implied as necessary to prevent and detect such malfeasance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer compensation and buyback standards in enforcement resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforcement settlements can require manufacturers to offer substantial compensation and buyback programs for affected owners (e.g., VW offered buybacks and compensation in the U.S.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settlements typically specify eligibility, compensation amounts, and buyback terms; these remedies are used to redress consumer harm from misrepresented emissions and performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact assessment standards linking emissions to public health
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies cited estimate population exposure and attributable mortalities from NOx pollution (e.g., 3,000 deaths per year in London attributed to air pollution), used to contextualize the public-health significance of emissions non-compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-health impact assessments reinforce the seriousness of emissions violations and inform regulatory and political urgency in enforcement.
